fired.name: Rate of joins without indexes

fired.id: Rate of reading first index entry
fired.name: Rate of reading first index entry
fired.issue: The rate of reading the first index entry is high.
fired.recommendation: This usually indicates frequent full index scans. Full index scans are faster than table scans but require lots of CPU cycles in big tables, if those tables that have or had high volumes of UPDATEs and DELETEs, running 'OPTIMIZE TABLE' might reduce the amount of and/or speed up full index scans. Other than that full index scans can only be reduced by rewriting queries.

fired.name: Rate of reading fixed position

fired.id: Rate of reading next table row

fired.name: Temp disk rate

notfired.name: InnoDB log size
notfired.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
notfired.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set innodb_log_file_size to 25% of innodb_buffer_pool_size. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
notfired.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at 75% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%

notfired.name: InnoDB buffer pool size
notfired.issue: Your InnoDB buffer pool is fairly small.
notfired.recommendation: The InnoDB buffer pool has a profound impact on performance for InnoDB tables. Assign all your remaining memory to this buffer. For database servers that use solely InnoDB as storage engine and have no other services (e.g. a web server) running, you may set this as high as 80% of your available memory. If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. If it is set too high, your system will start swapping, which decreases performance significantly. See also this article
notfired.justification: You are currently using 838.8608% of your memory for the InnoDB buffer pool. This rule fires if you are assigning less than 60%, however this might be perfectly adequate for your system if you don't have much InnoDB tables or other services running on the same machine.

notfired.recommendation: Clients are usually aborted when they did not close their connection to MySQL properly. This can be due to network issues or code not closing a database handler properly. Check your network and code.
notfired.justification: Aborted client rate is at 1 per hour, this value should be less than 1 per hour

notfired.name: InnoDB log size
notfired.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
notfired.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set innodb_log_file_size to 25% of innodb_buffer_pool_size. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
notfired.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at 75% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%

notfired.name: InnoDB buffer pool size
notfired.issue: Your InnoDB buffer pool is fairly small.
notfired.recommendation: The InnoDB buffer pool has a profound impact on performance for InnoDB tables. Assign all your remaining memory to this buffer. For database servers that use solely InnoDB as storage engine and have no other services (e.g. a web server) running, you may set this as high as 80% of your available memory. If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. If it is set too high, your system will start swapping, which decreases performance significantly. See also this article
notfired.justification: You are currently using 838.8608% of your memory for the InnoDB buffer pool. This rule fires if you are assigning less than 60%, however this might be perfectly adequate for your system if you don't have much InnoDB tables or other services running on the same machine.

fired.id: Rate of reading first index entry
fired.name: Rate of reading first index entry
fired.issue: The rate of reading the first index entry is high.
fired.recommendation: This usually indicates frequent full index scans. Full index scans are faster than table scans but require lots of CPU cycles in big tables, if those tables that have or had high volumes of UPDATEs and DELETEs, running 'OPTIMIZE TABLE' might reduce the amount of and/or speed up full index scans. Other than that full index scans can only be reduced by rewriting queries.
fired.justification: Index scans average: 1.25 per minute, this value should be less than 1 per hour

fired.name: Query cache fragmentation
fired.issue: The query cache is considerably fragmented.
fired.recommendation: Severe fragmentation is likely to (further) increase Qcache_lowmem_prunes. This might be caused by many Query cache low memory prunes due to query_cache_size being too small. For a immediate but short lived fix you can flush the query cache (might lock the query cache for a long time). Carefully adjusting query_cache_min_res_unit to a lower value might help too, e.g. you can set it to the average size of your queries in the cache using this formula: (query_cache_size - qcache_free_memory) / qcache_queries_in_cache
fired.justification: The cache is currently fragmented by 80% , with 100% fragmentation meaning that the query cache is an alternating pattern of free and used blocks. This value should be below 20%.

fired.name: Query cache low memory prunes
fired.issue: Cached queries are removed due to low query cache memory from the query cache.
fired.recommendation: You might want to increase query_cache_size, however keep in mind that the overhead of maintaining the cache is likely to increase with its size, so do this in small increments and monitor the results.
fired.justification: The ratio of removed queries to inserted queries is 1%. The lower this value is, the better (This rules firing limit: 0.1%)

fired.name: Query cache min result size
fired.issue: The max size of the result set in the query cache is the default of 1 MiB.
fired.recommendation: Changing query_cache_limit (usually by increasing) may increase efficiency. This variable determines the maximum size a query result may have to be inserted into the query cache. If there are many query results above 1 MiB that are well cacheable (many reads, little writes) then increasing query_cache_limit will increase efficiency. Whereas in the case of many query results being above 1 MiB that are not very well cacheable (often invalidated due to table updates) increasing query_cache_limit might reduce efficiency.
fired.justification: query_cache_limit is set to 1 MiB

notfired.name: Rate of aborted clients

notfired.name: InnoDB log size
notfired.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
notfired.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set innodb_log_file_size to 25% of innodb_buffer_pool_size. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
notfired.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at 75% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%

notfired.name: InnoDB buffer pool size
notfired.issue: Your InnoDB buffer pool is fairly small.
notfired.recommendation: The InnoDB buffer pool has a profound impact on performance for InnoDB tables. Assign all your remaining memory to this buffer. For database servers that use solely InnoDB as storage engine and have no other services (e.g. a web server) running, you may set this as high as 80% of your available memory. If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. If it is set too high, your system will start swapping, which decreases performance significantly. See also this article
notfired.justification: You are currently using 3355.4432% of your memory for the InnoDB buffer pool. This rule fires if you are assigning less than 60%, however this might be perfectly adequate for your system if you don't have much InnoDB tables or other services running on the same machine.

fired.name: Query Cache usage
fired.issue: Less than 80% of the query cache is being utilized.
fired.recommendation: This might be caused by query_cache_limit being too low. Flushing the query cache might help as well.
fired.justification: The current ratio of free query cache memory to total query cache size is 2%. It should be above 80%

fired.name: Query cache fragmentation
fired.issue: The query cache is considerably fragmented.
fired.recommendation: Severe fragmentation is likely to (further) increase Qcache_lowmem_prunes. This might be caused by many Query cache low memory prunes due to query_cache_size being too small. For a immediate but short lived fix you can flush the query cache (might lock the query cache for a long time). Carefully adjusting query_cache_min_res_unit to a lower value might help too, e.g. you can set it to the average size of your queries in the cache using this formula: (query_cache_size - qcache_free_memory) / qcache_queries_in_cache
fired.justification: The cache is currently fragmented by 80% , with 100% fragmentation meaning that the query cache is an alternating pattern of free and used blocks. This value should be below 20%.

fired.name: Query cache low memory prunes
fired.issue: Cached queries are removed due to low query cache memory from the query cache.
fired.recommendation: You might want to increase query_cache_size, however keep in mind that the overhead of maintaining the cache is likely to increase with its size, so do this in small increments and monitor the results.
fired.justification: The ratio of removed queries to inserted queries is 1%. The lower this value is, the better (This rules firing limit: 0.1%)

fired.name: Query cache min result size
fired.issue: The max size of the result set in the query cache is the default of 1 MiB.
fired.recommendation: Changing query_cache_limit (usually by increasing) may increase efficiency. This variable determines the maximum size a query result may have to be inserted into the query cache. If there are many query results above 1 MiB that are well cacheable (many reads, little writes) then increasing query_cache_limit will increase efficiency. Whereas in the case of many query results being above 1 MiB that are not very well cacheable (often invalidated due to table updates) increasing query_cache_limit might reduce efficiency.
fired.justification: query_cache_limit is set to 1 MiB

notfired.name: InnoDB buffer pool size

If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. fired.name: Temp disk rate
fired.issue: Many temporary tables are being written to disk instead of being kept in memory.
fired.recommendation: Increasing max_heap_table_size and tmp_table_size might help. However some temporary tables are always being written to disk, independent of the value of these variables. To eliminate these you will have to rewrite your queries to avoid those conditions (Within a temporary table: Presence of a BLOB or TEXT column or presence of a column bigger than 512 bytes) as mentioned in the MySQL Documentation
fired.justification: Rate of temporary tables being written to disk: 12 per hour, this value should be less than 1 per hour

fired.id: Max % MyISAM key buffer ever used

fired.id: Percentage of index reads from memory

fired.name: Query cache efficiency (%)
fired.issue: Query cache not running efficiently, it has a low hit rate.
fired.recommendation: Consider increasing query_cache_limit.
fired.justification: The current query cache hit rate of 1% is below 20%

fired.name: Query Cache usage
fired.issue: Less than 80% of the query cache is being utilized.
fired.recommendation: This might be caused by query_cache_limit being too low. Flushing the query cache might help as well.
fired.justification: The current ratio of free query cache memory to total query cache size is 2%. It should be above 80%

fired.name: Query cache fragmentation
fired.issue: The query cache is considerably fragmented.
fired.recommendation: Severe fragmentation is likely to (further) increase Qcache_lowmem_prunes. This might be caused by many Query cache low memory prunes due to query_cache_size being too small. For a immediate but short lived fix you can flush the query cache (might lock the query cache for a long time). Carefully adjusting query_cache_min_res_unit to a lower value might help too, e.g. you can set it to the average size of your queries in the cache using this formula: (query_cache_size - qcache_free_memory) / qcache_queries_in_cache
fired.justification: The cache is currently fragmented by 80% , with 100% fragmentation meaning that the query cache is an alternating pattern of free and used blocks. This value should be below 20%.

fired.name: Query cache low memory prunes
fired.issue: Cached queries are removed due to low query cache memory from the query cache.
fired.recommendation: You might want to increase query_cache_size, however keep in mind that the overhead of maintaining the cache is likely to increase with its size, so do this in small increments and monitor the results.
fired.justification: The ratio of removed queries to inserted queries is 1%. The lower this value is, the better (This rules firing limit: 0.1%)

fired.name: Query cache min result size
fired.issue: The max size of the result set in the query cache is the default of 1 MiB.
fired.recommendation: Changing query_cache_limit (usually by increasing) may increase efficiency. This variable determines the maximum size a query result may have to be inserted into the query cache. If there are many query results above 1 MiB that are well cacheable (many reads, little writes) then increasing query_cache_limit will increase efficiency. Whereas in the case of many query results being above 1 MiB that are not very well cacheable (often invalidated due to table updates) increasing query_cache_limit might reduce efficiency.
fired.justification: query_cache_limit is set to 1 MiB

notfired.name: Is InnoDB disabled?
notfired.issue: You do not have InnoDB enabled.
notfired.recommendation: InnoDB is usually the better choice for table engines.
notfired.justification: have_innodb is set to 'value'

notfired.name: InnoDB log size
notfired.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
notfired.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set innodb_log_file_size to 25% of innodb_buffer_pool_size. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
notfired.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at 75% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%

notfired.name: InnoDB buffer pool size
notfired.issue: Your InnoDB buffer pool is fairly small.
notfired.recommendation: The InnoDB buffer pool has a profound impact on performance for InnoDB tables. Assign all your remaining memory to this buffer. For database servers that use solely InnoDB as storage engine and have no other services (e.g. a web server) running, you may set this as high as 80% of your available memory. If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. If it is set too high, your system will start swapping, which decreases performance significantly. See also this article
notfired.justification: You are currently using 1677.7216% of your memory for the InnoDB buffer pool. This rule fires if you are assigning less than 60%, however this might be perfectly adequate for your system if you don't have much InnoDB tables or other services running on the same machine.

notfired.name: InnoDB log size
notfired.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
notfired.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set innodb_log_file_size to 25% of innodb_buffer_pool_size. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
notfired.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at 75% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%

notfired.name: InnoDB buffer pool size
notfired.issue: Your InnoDB buffer pool is fairly small.
notfired.recommendation: The InnoDB buffer pool has a profound impact on performance for InnoDB tables. Assign all your remaining memory to this buffer. For database servers that use solely InnoDB as storage engine and have no other services (e.g. a web server) running, you may set this as high as 80% of your available memory. If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. If it is set too high, your system will start swapping, which decreases performance significantly. See also this article
notfired.justification: You are currently using 838.8608% of your memory for the InnoDB buffer pool. This rule fires if you are assigning less than 60%, however this might be perfectly adequate for your system if you don't have much InnoDB tables or other services running on the same machine.

fired.recommendation: This indicates that many queries need to sort results and/or do a full table scan, including join queries that do not use indexes. Add indexes where applicable.
fired.justification: Rate of reading fixed position average: 9 per hour, this value should be less than 1 per hour

fired.id: Rate of reading next table row
fired.name: Rate of reading next table row
fired.issue: The rate of reading the next table row is high.
fired.recommendation: This indicates that many queries are doing full table scans. Add indexes where applicable.
fired.justification: Rate of reading next table row: 22.22 per second, this value should be less than 1 per hour

fired.name: Temp disk rate
fired.issue: Many temporary tables are being written to disk instead of being kept in memory.
fired.recommendation: Increasing max_heap_table_size and tmp_table_size might help. However some temporary tables are always being written to disk, independent of the value of these variables. To eliminate these you will have to rewrite your queries to avoid those conditions (Within a temporary table: Presence of a BLOB or TEXT column or presence of a column bigger than 512 bytes) as mentioned in the MySQL Documentation
fired.justification: Rate of temporary tables being written to disk: 12 per hour, this value should be less than 1 per hour

fired.id: Max % MyISAM key buffer ever used
fired.name: Max % MyISAM key buffer ever used
fired.issue: MyISAM key buffer (index cache) % used is low.
fired.recommendation: You may need to decrease the size of key_buffer_size, re-examine your tables to see if indexes have been removed, or examine queries and expectations about what indexes are being used.
fired.justification: max % MyISAM key buffer ever used: 0%, this value should be above 95%

fired.id: Percentage of index reads from memory
fired.name: Percentage of index reads from memory
fired.issue: The % of indexes that use the MyISAM key buffer is low.
fired.recommendation: You may need to increase key_buffer_size.
fired.justification: Index reads from memory: 93%, this value should be above 95%

fired.name: Rate of table open
fired.issue: The rate of opening tables is high.
fired.recommendation: Opening tables requires disk I/O which is costly. Increasing table_open_cache might avoid this.
fired.justification: Opened table rate: 5 per minute, this value should be less than 10 per hour

fired.name: Rate of open files
fired.issue: The rate of opening files is high.
fired.recommendation: Consider increasing open_files_limit, and check the error log when restarting after changing open_files_limit.
fired.justification: Opened files rate: 20 per hour, this value should be less than 5 per hour

notfired.name: InnoDB log size
notfired.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
notfired.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set innodb_log_file_size to 25% of innodb_buffer_pool_size. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
notfired.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at 75% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%

notfired.name: InnoDB buffer pool size
notfired.issue: Your InnoDB buffer pool is fairly small.
notfired.recommendation: The InnoDB buffer pool has a profound impact on performance for InnoDB tables. Assign all your remaining memory to this buffer. For database servers that use solely InnoDB as storage engine and have no other services (e.g. a web server) running, you may set this as high as 80% of your available memory. If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. If it is set too high, your system will start swapping, which decreases performance significantly. See also this article
notfired.justification: You are currently using 838.8608% of your memory for the InnoDB buffer pool. This rule fires if you are assigning less than 60%, however this might be perfectly adequate for your system if you don't have much InnoDB tables or other services running on the same machine.
